To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

EPEC uses type III secretion to deliver a protein that activates host cell phosphatases, which then cause the actin cytoskeleton to disassemble, resulting in intimate adherence of the bacteria and the formation of actin pedestals.

EPEC induces a signaling pathway in the host cell which is required for the bacteria to adhere tightly to the cell surface and that EPEC induces an actin-based cytoskeletal rearrangement that leads to formation of an actin pedestal beneath the bacteria.
the pathogenesis of EPEC infection is emerging as paradigm of a multistage, microorganism-host interaction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms by which EPEC causes diarrhea and the role of these interactions in the pathogenesis of other bacterial diarrheal diseases.
the mechanisms of EPEC pathogenesis, with a focus on the role of the type III secretion system in the interaction between bacteria and host cells.
the mechanisms that underlie the pathogenesis of EPEC infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EPEC are able to colonize the gut of a susceptible host by means of a complex and coordinated interaction with the host epithelium.
EPEC is a pathogen that causes disease by a complex interaction of virulence factors and host cell factors.

enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC), like Shigella, Yersinia and Salmonella, has developed an arsenal of virulence factors that enable the bacteria to invade the host cell cytoplasm, subvert its metabolism and cause disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the type III secretion system is a molecular syringe that injects bacterial effector molecules into the cytoplasm of the target host cell.
EPEC is an excellent model for understanding the mechanisms of bacterial adherence to and entry into host cells, and the molecular basis for the pathogenesis of EPEC-induced diarrhea.
EPEC induces actin cytoskeletal rearrangements that result in the formation of actin pedestals beneath the bacteria, which in turn leads to the development of microcolony-like clusters of bacteria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
enteropathogenic Esch. coli (EPEC)-mediated signaling is required for the formation of the characteristic attaching-effacing lesion.

the pathogenesis of enteric diseases caused by enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic E. coli is a complex multistage process involving a number of virulence factors, and that the host cell is an integral part of this process.
the host cell is not a passive recipient of the EPEC virulence determinants.
